card.hook: Everyone at Lalbagh seems to end up on the same patch of grass, phone up, shuffling left and right like they're parking a car. They're all after the Glass House, the garden's most photographed building, and the lawn gives you plenty of room to get it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the south lawn, in front of the Glass House, and face the iron-and-glass facade. Walk a few steps left or right until the dome sits in the middle of your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 1x. That fits the whole facade and dome with a bit of grass in front. If the lawn is busy and you have to stand close, tap 0.5x to keep the dome in, and hold your phone level so the sides don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on the centre line, then tap the glass and slide the brightness down a touch so it doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before about 10 AM. The softer light keeps the glass from blowing out to white.
card.selfie_here: Try the side steps of the Glass House: use the front camera (tap 0.5x if yours has it) and keep the ironwork and sky behind you. Visitors recommend these steps for shots of the building, so treat it as a good bet rather than a guarantee.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the open lawn south of the Glass House, facing the building, while you stand in front of the facade so the dome fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones are prohibited without special aviation clearance. Lalbagh is a gated garden, so check the official site before you go, and check on the day whether phone photography is free. It gets very sunny, so bring a hat and sunscreen.
card.challenge: Get the dome dead centre on the grid line, then wait for someone to stroll across the lawn and add a little scale to the shot.
card.good_to_know: Lalbagh is a large botanical garden in Bangalore, and guides call the Glass House its most photographed building. The inside is normally closed unless a flower show is on, so plan to shoot the outside. Once you have your shot, head to Lalbagh Rock for a wide view over the treetops with a 16th-century watchtower, or to the lake bridge for tree reflections.

card.hook: Turrets, climbing plants on the walls and a big green lawn: you could swear you'd taken a wrong turn and ended up in England. Bangalore Palace is built like a small English castle, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Palace Road, right in front of the ornate main gate, and face the gateway. The palace itself is to the north-east, so you'll get the first glimpse of the facade beyond the gate.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the gate and that first peek of the palace. Tap 0.5x if you want the whole gateway and lawns in one frame, then 2x or more (depends on your phone) for the turrets and gate details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the gate in the foreground with the palace sitting beyond it, and keep your phone level so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: Golden hour is worth a try, when the low light is soft and warm on the gate and facade. The grounds host concerts, fairs and weddings, so the scene can change from day to day.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the old Gothic windows on the outside of the palace with the building behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it, so the windows and turrets fit over your shoulder. The open lawn in front of the palace works too.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by, ask them to stand on the lawn facing the building, and stand in front of the facade so the palace is behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Interior photography is restricted, so ask at the entrance before taking your phone inside. One guide mentions a photography fee and a token at entry, with phone photos costing less. Professional shoots need prior permission, and the palace is privately managed.
card.challenge: Can you get the gate in the foreground and one turret poking out behind it, all lined up on the gridlines? Bonus points if the sky stays properly blue.
card.good_to_know: Bangalore Palace was commissioned in 1873 for Chamarajendra Wadiyar X, the Maharaja of Mysore. Its design is based on Windsor Castle, in the Tudor Revival style. It has about 34 rooms and sits roughly 5.3 km north of the city centre.

card.hook: Picture 40,000 people packed into one giant bowl, with red and yellow everywhere you look. That's Chinnaswamy on a big match day, and it's a lot to fit into one photo.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map marks the stadium itself. The best view is from the upper tier of the G stand, looking across the whole ground, but you'll need a ticket for that. If you're only outside, stand on Queens Road by gates 1 and 2 and face the big lettering on the front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bowl in, then switch to 1x for a more natural view of the field. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details like the pitch or the scoreboard.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the green field filling the bottom half and the stands and sky above, then tap the field and drag the slider to make it a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the stands.
card.best_time: Go on a ticketed match or event day for the full atmosphere. If it's an evening game under floodlights, switch on night mode and rest your phone against the rail or your arm. For the outside sign, pick a quieter non-event day, because crowds build up fast at the gates.
card.selfie_here: Outside by the big 'Chinnaswamy Stadium' sign on the facade near Gate 1-2. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold the phone a bit lower so the lettering sits over your shoulder. Only one traveller blog names this spot, so check it looks right when you arrive.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are on the not-permitted list (reported for IPL 2026 matches), and filming the match itself is generally not allowed, though a phone camera is fine. Rules can vary by event, so check the official site before you go. Always respect railings and security tape.
card.challenge: Pan slowly with panorama mode and see if you can capture the whole curve of the bowl without a wobble. Bonus points if the pitch sits dead centre.
card.good_to_know: Work on the stadium began in 1970, and the first Test was played here in November 1974. It's home to Karnataka's teams and Royal Challengers Bangalore, whose colours give the place its bold look. It was also the first cricket stadium in the world to use solar panels for much of its electricity.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map marks the stadium itself. card.hook: Picture a red-brick library sitting behind a sea of rose beds, right in the middle of a busy city. That's the Cubbon Park shot, and it takes about ten seconds to find.
card.stand_here: Stand on the front lawn of the State Central Library, beside the rose beds inside the park. Face the red-brick building across the roses and let the winding paths lead your eye to it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the library with the rose beds in front. Go to 0.5x to fit the whole building and the paths in, or 2x and up (depending on your phone) for brickwork and roses.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red brick, then slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the brick stays rich.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people on the lawns. Early morning is also when walkers and joggers fill the shady avenues, so expect company.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Bandstand area and stand on the lawns beside the cast-iron octagonal Bandstand. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the Bandstand over your shoulder. For a fairytale backdrop, try the bamboo grove and the bridge in the same part of the park.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the approach to the red Attara Kacheri gateway at the park entrance, facing the entrance, so the park fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography for personal use is free and permitted throughout the park. Don't take close-up photos of people without their consent. One reviewer advises against walking in the park in the evenings.
card.challenge: Find a curving path, put it in the bottom of your frame, and get the library at the end with one rose poking into the corner.
card.good_to_know: Cubbon Park was laid out in 1870 and named after Sir Mark Cubbon, a long-serving commissioner. It started at around 100 acres and is now reported to cover about 300. In 1927 it became Sri Chamarajendra Park, and it's formerly known as Cubbon Park. Attara Kacheri, built in 1864 and now the High Court, stands at the park's edge.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the front lawn of the State Central Library, beside the rose beds inside the park. Face the red-brick building across the roses and let the winding paths lead your eye to it.

card.hook: Here's the trick with UB City: it's so big and so straight-edged that one slightly tilted phone makes the whole thing look like it's about to topple over. Get across the road and let it tower.
card.stand_here: Stand on Vittal Mallya Road, on the opposite side of the road from the mall, and face the building so its lower part fills your frame with the street running across the bottom. If you're walking over, the MG Road-Brigade Road junction is about 1.8 km away.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tall building and the street in one frame. Then try 1x for a tidier, less stretched look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the glass and the arched upper section.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so it stands up straight.
card.best_time: Go in daylight for the clearest view of the glass and lines. After dark, switch on night mode and hold your phone steady against something solid.
card.selfie_here: Try the Vishveshwar Museum side of the road with the UB City arch behind you, using the front camera (and 0.5x if your phone has it). One travel blog suggests this spot, but it's an older tip and says the whole building is hard to fit in, so check it still works when you get there. Inside, the open-air Piazza on Vittal Mallya Road is another option, with the building's architecture around you.
card.ask_someone: For a wider shot with the towers behind you, the Sri Kanteerava Stadium side gives a long view of UB City, so you could ask someone there to take your picture, but check the spot on site first.
card.rules_and_safety: The street view is from a public road, but shop interiors in the mall may restrict photography, and professional shoots need permission from mall management, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the traffic and people, then get a street so clean the building looks like it's all yours. Bonus points for a frame where every vertical line sits perfectly on the grid.
card.good_to_know: UB City is a cluster of six buildings on about 13 acres, built by the UB Group together with Prestige Group. It mixes offices, luxury shops and service apartments, and it has four towers. One of them, UB Tower, has a rooftop helipad. It stands opposite Cubbon Park, so glass and steel sit right beside one of the city's green spaces.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Vittal Mallya Road, on the opposite side of the road from the mall, and face the building so its lower part fills your frame with the street running across the bottom. If you're walking over, the MG Road-Brigade Road junction is about 1.8 km away.

card.hook: Here's the thing about a temple this big: you'll keep stepping backwards, trying to fit it all in, and the courtyard is where that finally works. The gold-topped bits catch the light, so you'll want them in the frame.
card.stand_here: Head for the main grand entrance and the outer courtyards in front of the temple on Hare Krishna Hill. The phone icon on the map is right there. Face the front facade and use the open courtyard to step back.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the facade and entrance as your eyes see them. Switch to 0.5x in the courtyards to get the whole front and the open space around it. Go to 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) for the carvings and the gold-topped features.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, keep the facade centred and hold your phone level so the building's vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Weekday mornings are the quietest, so you get cleaner shots of the facade. If you stay later, the evening fountains by the pond are worth seeing, and night mode helps with them.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the kalyani (the sacred pond) with your front camera and let the temple sit behind your shoulder, ideally with its reflection in the water. Another good spot is the outdoor approach at the grand entrance, under the illuminated arches and water jets. Neither spot has a set direction to face, so move around until the temple fits behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the grand entrance approach, ask them to stand back in front of the gopuram, and pose yourself so the gopuram and the gold-plated flag post both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: No photos inside the main sanctum or prayer halls, and no flash in the worship area. The outer courtyards, entrance and gardens are fine for pictures. Drones are not allowed. Expect security checks at the entrances, and keep an eye on your valuables when it's crowded. If you're unsure about a spot, ask a temple volunteer.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole temple, then one close-up of the carving, and see if a friend can guess where the close-up came from.
card.good_to_know: ISKCON Temple Bangalore is one of the largest Krishna temples in the world. It was inaugurated in May 1997 by India's then president, Shankar Dayal Sharma. It's dedicated to Radha Krishna and has six shrines, and the gold-plated flag post (17 m) and kalash shikhara (8.5 m) are the stars of the skyline.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the main grand entrance and the outer courtyards in front of the temple on Hare Krishna Hill. The phone icon on the map is right there. Face the front facade and use the open courtyard to step back.

card.hook: Forty-five steps, 12 tall columns and one huge dome: Vidhana Soudha doesn't do small. It was meant to be a 'people's palace', and from across the road you can see why.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ambedkar Veedhi, the road facing the front of the building, on the road side opposite the front. Face the building straight on so the dome sits in the middle of your screen. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of traffic.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole front, the steps and the sky above the dome. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the dome, the columns or the emblem on top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on the middle line so both sides of the building match.
card.best_time: Early morning, around 7-8 AM, is quiet for traffic. The building is lit mainly on Sunday and public-holiday evenings, so a weekday evening may find it dark. Check on the day and choose between a calm morning and a lit evening.
card.selfie_here: Reviewers mention a small road-level selfie point on Ambedkar Veedhi, right opposite the building, where it looms behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit the wide front, and keep the dome over your shoulder. Take it from the pavement, not out in the traffic.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the street from the building, near the Karnataka High Court (Attara Kacheri), so the whole landmark fits in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a high-security zone, so don't cross the barricades or go through the gates without a pre-booked guided tour. Shoot from the sidewalk along the perimeter fence, follow any staff instructions, and keep your phone pointed at the building, not at people.
card.challenge: Fit all 12 columns and the dome in one shot, then count them at home to check you got every one.
card.good_to_know: Vidhana Soudha was finished in 1956 in the Neo-Dravidian style, with pink and black granite that gives it a warm look. The dome is about 18 metres across and topped with the State Emblem of India. The whole complex covers around 60 acres and is described as the largest state legislature and secretariat building in India.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ambedkar Veedhi, the road facing the front of the building, on the road side opposite the front. Face the building straight on so the dome sits in the middle of your screen. Stay on the pavement and keep clear of traffic.

card.hook: Picture a bright red courthouse glowing against green trees, with a white granite palace right behind you. That's Attara Kacheri, and the red-against-white clash is the whole photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Dr. Ambedkar Veedhi, on the Vidhana Soudha side of the road, and face the red front of Attara Kacheri. It lies to the south-east of you, with the trees of Cubbon Park rising behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole red front with the trees behind it. If the pavement is too narrow to fit it all, drop to zoom 0.5x. Go to zoom 2x for the columns and the symmetrical middle of the building.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, line the centre of the building up with the middle of the frame, and keep your phone level so the columns don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning and late afternoon are described as pleasant times to visit, and they work well for photos too.
card.selfie_here: Head into Cubbon Park, on the park side of the High Court, and use the front camera with the red building over your shoulder. Guides don't name an exact bench or path, so wander until the red front fills the background. If it won't fit, try zoom 0.5x on the front camera, if your phone has it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Ambedkar Veedhi main road facing the High Court, stepping back far enough to fit more of the front in. You stand with the red building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working court, so photograph the outside only. Photography is prohibited inside, and phones aren't allowed in. Follow security instructions, stay out of restricted areas, and be discreet near the entrances. Check the frontage is clear before you go, as construction has blocked the view on at least one visit.
card.challenge: Get the red front and the white Vidhana Soudha into your story: take one shot facing the court, then turn around and take one facing the palace.
card.good_to_know: Attara Kacheri was built between 1864 and 1868 and is a two-storey neoclassical building of stone and brick. In 1982 there was a proposal to demolish it. The first public interest litigation ever filed in the court was brought to stop that, and the plan was dropped in 1985. It was later renovated and extended with new blocks in the same style.

card.hook: Painted shopfronts, bright shutters, shoppers and street vendors all squeezed into one view: Commercial Street never does quiet, and that's exactly why your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement right where the phone icon sits on Commercial Street, in Tasker Town. Face along the line of shopfronts so the street leads the eye into your picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for natural-looking street scenes. Pop to 0.5x to squeeze the whole row of shopfronts into the narrow street. Then try 2x or 5x (if your phone has it) to pick out one colourful shutter or a vendor's stall.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and run the line of shopfronts along one third of the frame. Then tap a bright shopfront and nudge it a touch darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go on a weekday morning, when the light is softer and there are fewer people. It's the easiest time to get a clear view.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement at the start of the street, by Sri Krishna Diamonds and Jewellery, or the corner where OPH Road meets Kamraj Road. Nobody lists either as an official photo point, but both put the street behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more shopfronts over your shoulder, and hold your phone a bit higher.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep wallets and purses secure, as things can go missing in the bustle. Ask first before taking close-ups of people or stalls, and note that commercial shoots may need permission from shops.
card.challenge: Find the brightest shutter on the street and catch a shopper walking past it, with no one blocking the colour.
card.good_to_know: Commercial Street is one of the oldest and busiest shopping streets in Bangalore. It runs between OPH Road and K Kamraj Road, and the shopping spills into side lanes like Dispensary Road and Abrahim Sahab Street. Parking is very limited, so expect people in every shot. If you want something calmer and older-feeling, Russell Market in Shivajinagar is nearby, though it doesn't show Commercial Street itself.

card.hook: There's a huge granite Nandi bull in Basavanagudi, and the rocky outcrop under his temple is half the charm. Get the big view from the rock first, then go and say hello to him up close.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x on the rock to fit in the trees, the watchtower and the town. Go to 1x for a natural view, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the temple and rooftops in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line, then use a tree branch or the watchtower as a frame in front.
card.best_time: Golden hour is the guide favourite for this area. Sources also mention sunset views from the top of the rock.
card.selfie_here: Climb to the top of Bugle Rock near Kempe Gowda's watch tower, where sources describe panoramic city views. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the view over your shoulder, and check your screen to see whether the temple sneaks into the frame.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the Bull Temple entrance with the gateway tower of sculpted deities behind you, and ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back in the outer area to take your photo.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine in the outer courtyard and the park, but not in the inner sanctum, so ask temple staff if you're unsure. The nearby Ganesha temple doesn't allow photos inside either. Please don't photograph devotees at prayer, drones are generally not permitted, and dress respectfully because it's a working place of worship.
card.challenge: Take two photos: a wide scene from the rock, then a tight portrait of the Nandi with the carved walls and roof around him. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The Bull Temple is also called Dodda Basavana Gudi, and it's famous for its huge granite Nandi bull. It sits on a rocky outcrop, which is part of why it photographs so well. In Bugle Rock Park, the rock with its watchtower is named as the park's main attraction.

card.hook: Picture a whole two-storey palace made of teak, with a lawn rolled out in front of it like a green carpet. That's Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace, and it's a gift for your phone.
card.stand_here: Start on the front lawn, where the phone icon on the map sits in the palace garden. Face the palace so the whole facade of arches, slim wooden pillars and balconies fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the full facade. If you're close and can't fit it all in, try zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x for the carved pillars and balconies.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the pillars so the building stays nice and straight, with a band of lawn along the bottom.
card.best_time: Go when the light is soft and the sun isn't sitting right behind the building. That way the teak keeps its warm colour instead of turning into a dark shape.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the garden lawn in front of the palace, with the wooden facade behind you and the entrance gate ahead. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a little higher so the arches show over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the lawn across the courtyard from the front facade, then stand in front of the palace yourself, so they get the whole building in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography rules vary here, so check the entry rules with the Archaeological Survey of India before you go. The museum galleries may have restrictions and flash may not be allowed, so look for signs. The staircases and some pillars are weak, and you shouldn't touch the walls covered by glass.
card.challenge: Get one shot with the facade perfectly level and a neat strip of green lawn below it, then one close-up of a carved pillar. Bonus points if you can spot the balconies where Tipu is said to have held court.
card.good_to_know: Hyder Ali began the palace in 1781, inside the walls of Bangalore Fort, and it was finished in 1791 in Tipu Sultan's time. It was Tipu's summer residence, and he is believed to have held court from the upper-floor balconies. The ground floor is now a small museum, looked after by the Archaeological Survey of India.

card.hook: Ulsoor Lake has a neat trick: when the water goes still, the trees and the Bangalore skyline turn up upside down in it. All you have to do is wait for the ripples to stop.
card.stand_here: Head to the eastern bank of Ulsoor Lake, near the trees, and face the water. Local guides name this shore as the place where the trees and the city skyline show up as reflections.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of water, trees and a slice of skyline. Go to 0.5x for more sky and a bigger sweep of the bank, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single tree or an island.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the water's edge on the lower third line, so the reflection fills the bottom half of your photo.
card.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are best. The light is soft and the water is usually at its stillest, so the reflections look their sharpest.
card.selfie_here: Try the northern promenade, on the walkway along the lake's edge. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the water and sunset sky behind you. The eastern bank near the trees is a good second spot, with the trees and skyline over your shoulder. Guides recommend both shores for sunset and scenery photos, so check the framing when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the lake are run by the Madras Engineer Group and the rest by the city corporation, so not every shoreline is open to walkers. Some of the surroundings were reported to be under renovation, so check local signs on the day. One reviewer said some sections of the walkway railing are broken, so keep children close.
card.challenge: Take two shots of the same tree: a wide one with the skyline, then a close one of just the tree and its reflection. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Ulsoor Lake, also called Halasuru Lake, is one of Bangalore's biggest lakes. It covers about 50 hectares and has several small islands. It goes back to Kempe Gowda's time, but the shape you see today was created by Lewin Bentham Bowring, a Commissioner of Bangalore.

card.hook: Where else can you see a jet engine, a full-size Wright Brothers' Flyer and a moving Spinosaurus on the same afternoon, all tucked into a leafy park? The Visvesvaraya Museum in Cubbon Park is a big, photogenic building, and that's before you go inside.

card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the Delhi Gate's carved stonework with the gate filling the background behind you. One guide calls it the prime photo spot at the fort. The lawn inside also works: use the front camera, try 0.5x, and let the old walls and gate sit over your shoulder.

card.rules_and_safety: One 2022 blog says photography is fine inside but photoshoots and photoshoot gear aren't allowed, so keep it to your phone and check the current Archaeological Survey of India rules before you go. The fort sits on a busy, crowded street, so keep an eye on your belongings.
card.challenge: Get the gate in the top half, the lawn in the bottom half and straight walls, all in one shot. Then take the same photo at 0.5x and pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: Kempe Gowda I began this fort in 1537 as a mud fort, and Hyder Ali rebuilt it in stone in 1761. Lord Cornwallis's British East India Company troops took it on 21 March 1791 by breaching the wall near the Delhi Gate, and a marble plaque marks the spot. The fort once ran about a mile around, so the Delhi Gate and two bastions are just a small piece of it.

card.hook: Pale columns, a dome and a tower, with MG Road traffic rumbling past. It looks like a slice of London got dropped into Bangalore, and the street view is the one everyone remembers.
card.stand_here: Stand on Mahatma Gandhi Road, across from the cathedral's front, and face the portico. You'll be looking roughly south at the portico, columns and tower, with the tree-lined compound around them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the portico, columns and tower in one go. Go to 0.5x only if you're too close, and try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the top of the tower or the columns.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale stonework, then slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go outside service times and skip the main Sunday service at 10:30 AM. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the front.
card.selfie_here: Stay out on the street side and use the front camera at 0.5x. Hold it at arm's length and tilt it up a little so the tower rises over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Mahatma Gandhi Road facing the portico and shoot you with the tree-lined front behind you, but check the spot on the map first.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside may be restricted, so be discreet and ask staff if you're unsure. Skip the flash and don't take photos during services.
card.challenge: Switch on gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, and let a tree frame each side. Take a few shots in a row so one comes out free of traffic.
card.good_to_know: St. Mark's began as a garrison church for the East India Company's Madras Army. The foundation stone was laid in 1808 and it was consecrated in 1816. After a fire in 1923 and a collapse in 1924 it was rebuilt, and the version you see today was finished in 1927 in an English Baroque style inspired by St Paul's Cathedral in London.

card.hook: Here's a building that's trying to be an island. It sits near Cubbon Park with water and lotuses around its base, and it's low, solid and very modernist. Check the sign first, because plenty of people mistake it for the Bangalore Museum next door.

card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon. The light is softer and the shadows show off the shape of the building.
card.selfie_here: Try the bridge over the lotus pond on the walk from the Government Museum to the gallery entrance, which is described as scenic. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x and see if you can get the gallery over your shoulder. No guide confirms the building fits behind you there, so check on site.
card.ask_someone: One travel guide suggests the Kasturba Road pavement, facing the red heritage façade, so you could ask someone there to take your photo, but check the building name to be sure which one is in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography without flash is reported as allowed, but selfies are generally restricted inside the galleries. One review says no photos inside the twin museums at all, so the sources disagree. Check on the day, and keep your belongings secure when it's crowded.
card.challenge: Wait for someone to cross the approach and catch them in your shot, so the building looks properly big.
card.good_to_know: The gallery shows work by K. Venkatappa (1886-1965), one of Karnataka's best-known artists, plus collections of KK Hebbar and the sculptor Rajaram. The foundation stone was laid on 24 November 1967 and the building was finished in 1975. It was designed to look like an artificial island with a moat and lotus pond, and only three of the five planned floors were built, which gives it that low, solid shape.

card.hook: Picture a long row of columns and round arches, all standing in line like they're posing for a class photo. That's the Government Museum on Kasturba Road, and your phone is going to love it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right at the Government Museum on Kasturba Road. Face the façade and keep the portico in the middle of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole front. If you're too close to step back, switch to zoom 0.5x and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the column tops and arches.

card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the front looks less harsh than at midday.
card.selfie_here: Pop into the courtyard in front of the red façade, or stand among the flowers in the garden around the building. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and keep the red building behind you over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Kasturba Road side of the building and step back far enough to fit the whole façade, while you pose in the courtyard or garden with the building behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is prohibited inside the museum, so keep your photos and selfies to the outside and the garden. Exterior items and statues outside can be photographed. Keep your belongings secure during crowded hours. The museum has been reported closed for renovation, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one perfectly symmetrical from the centre, then one from a step to the side to show how deep those columns go. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: The museum was founded in 1865 and first sat in the old Cantonment jail building. It moved into this purpose-built home in 1877 and is one of the oldest museums in India. Inside is the Halmidi inscription, the earliest known Kannada inscription (450 AD).

card.hook: Here's a secret: the best shot of St Mary's isn't at the front door. It's from the end of a busy market street, where the tower pops up over the stalls like it's waiting for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on Commercial Street and face north-west, then walk towards the church from the Commercial Street end. The tower will appear at the far end of the street with market life in front of it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the tower sits small at the end of the street with the market around it. Tap 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the tower closer. Save 0.5x for when you reach the church and want the whole front and spire in one frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, then tap the tower and drag a little darker so the sky stays pale blue instead of white.
card.best_time: Go on a weekday, early if you can, when the street is quieter. Sundays, feast days and the September feast are the busiest, and processions can block your view of the tower.
card.selfie_here: Head to Russel Market Square, which sits directly opposite the basilica. Stand in the square with the tower behind you, use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the church in over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on the Shivajinagar road side of the front façade, far enough away to fit the whole tower in, while you pose in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside may be restricted during Mass and prayer services, so ask the church authorities first. Please don't use flash, especially during services. Drones are generally not permitted in and around religious sites.
card.challenge: Take one shot where a stall or a passing face sits in the foreground and the tower lands neatly on a gridline. Bonus points if the street seems to lead you straight to it.
card.good_to_know: St Mary's is a Gothic-style church in Shivajinagar, the area once known as Blackpally. It was rebuilt between 1856 and 1882 and consecrated on 8 September 1882. In 1973 it became a minor basilica, the first church in Karnataka to hold that status.
